150b431a10.q: What safety risks emerged from scaffold construction methods using boom lifts instead of conventional hanging methods?
150b431a10.a: When a scaffold was built using a boom lift rather than conventional construction as a hanging scaffold, fittings were not all done up properly. Terry…
f: Boom lifts introduced a critical construction flaw: not all fittings were properly completed during assembly. When a scaffold was built using a boom lift rather than conventional hanging methods, the transom fitting could go unfinished while the ledger fitting was secured , leaving tubes vulnerable to collapse.

Terry Riggs witnessed this danger firsthand in Port Hedland around 1998. At a 70-metre tower, a tube dropped because while the ledger fitting had been tightened, the transom fitting remained incomplete. The tube fell with terrifying speed—saved from catastrophe only by a vessel's protrusion that broke its fall. Without that chance obstruction, Riggs and his off-sider would have come off the scaffold entirely.

This wasn't an isolated mishap. The shift from conventional hanging scaffold methods to boom lift assembly fundamentally changed how work was sequenced on site. In hanging scaffold construction, workers had time and physical access to verify every fitting was properly torqued before moving to the next stage. Boom lifts accelerated the process but introduced gaps in the workflow where supervisors might assume fittings were complete without verification.

As discussed at length in this podcast episode , the real danger lay in the assumption. A ledger fitting done up could mask an incomplete transom fitting on the opposite side of the joint, creating an asymmetric load condition that destabilized the entire vertical support.
"If you can't get on with people, you're no good. Doesn't matter if you're a super scaffolder. We'll just get rid of you and get two other people."

Terry Riggs — Contract Scaffolder. Riggs started in the building and construction industry in 1971 as a builder's labourer in Sale, East Gippsland, before transitioning to scaffolding ten years later. He gained expertise in complex metal scaffold construction through major projects including Barry Beach offshore construction from 1978 to 1983, obtained both scaffolding and rigging qualifications, and has been a contract scaffolder across commercial and suburban construction sites throughout Victoria and Western Australia since the 1980s.

5138931a4c.q: What structural failures occur when scaffold standards are not staggered properly?
5138931a4c.a: When standards are not staggered and joins all align on one level, the scaffold can fail catastrophically. Terry saw a clattered demolition scaffold on…
f: When scaffold standards are not staggered and all joins align on a single level, the entire structure can collapse catastrophically , with standards pulling out of their connections and the scaffold hanging into the street or surrounding area.

This structural principle lies at the heart of scaffold safety, yet it represents one of the most dangerous oversights in construction. Terry Riggs witnessed this failure firsthand during his decades of work across Australian building sites.
A Real Collapse: Russell Street, 1980s

During the 1980s, Terry Riggs observed a scaffolding disaster on Russell Street that exemplified this structural weakness. The scaffold had been erected without proper staggering of the standard joints—meaning every vertical post connection aligned at the same height.

The result was immediate and catastrophic: the standards pulled out of their spigots on the building side , causing the entire scaffolding to hang loose into Russell Street below. This wasn't a minor failure or a minor slump. This was a complete structural breach that exposed workers and the public to severe danger.

Such incidents reveal more than just an engineering mistake. They signal, as discussed in the episode , a loss of the skill and knowledge that had previously governed how scaffolds were properly erected—knowledge passed through hands-on experience and custom practice among experienced scaffolders.

d5ce19cd85.q: How did WorkCover compensation address the lost income and social isolation experienced by construction workers during extended work-related injuries?
d5ce19cd85.a: According to Riggs, while WorkCover paid enough to live on, the compensation could not replace the majority of a construction worker's wage, which comes…
f: WorkCover paid enough to live on, but it couldn't replace the majority of a construction worker's wage—which comes from overtime and other conditions rather than the base hourly rate. Social isolation during years of recovery added a crushing psychological cost that no compensation formula could address.
The Gap Between Base Pay and Real Earnings

The majority of a construction worker's wage isn't his hourly rate —it's his overtime and other conditions. As explained in this episode of Creatures of the Industry , Terry Riggs sustained a scaphoid fracture that kept him out of work for two years. While the compensation covered basic living expenses, it bore no relation to the actual income he lost through missed overtime.

Construction work operates on a different financial structure than most employment. The base rate is merely the foundation; real earning power comes from extended hours, shift premiums, and project-specific allowances. WorkCover assessments, however, typically calculate benefits based on ordinary time earnings—a fundamental mismatch that leaves injured workers financially adrift.
Isolation Beyond the Paycheck

The financial shortfall was only half the story. Two years without work meant two years without the social structure that defines site life . Riggs described the psychological toll plainly: "You haven't got enough money to buy yourself whiskey and you haven't got the usual social interaction and that's a big change."

1ada068e5f.q: How did the Longford Gas Plant disaster in 1998 create employment opportunities and change working conditions for construction workers in Gippsland?
1ada068e5f.a: After the Longford gas plant explosion that killed five people, Riggs secured work with Fleur Daniel on the remediation and construction job to make the…
f: After the explosion that killed five people, the remediation and reconstruction of the Longford Gas Plant became one of the most substantial construction jobs available to workers in the region . The state government invested heavily in the project, providing workers with improved conditions: 12-hour shifts, on-site accommodation at 90 Mile Beach, a dedicated canteen, and shuttle bus access across the massive facility.
Remediation work as rare opportunity

Terry Riggs secured work with Fleur Daniel on the remediation and construction phases that followed the 1998 disaster. He describes this as one of only half a dozen truly good jobs throughout his entire career in construction. The scale of the project was significant enough to absorb substantial numbers of skilled workers across multiple trades.

Though the state government's flooding of resources created the opportunity, it also came with trade-offs. Workers faced long 12-hour shifts punctuated by periods of little work , a pattern typical of large-scale industrial remediation where mobilization and demobilization cycles left gaps in productivity.
Infrastructure for the workforce

What distinguished this job from many others was the employer's provision of comprehensive support systems. Workers received accommodation directly on the 90 Mile Beach site , removing the burden of finding housing in the surrounding area. A canteen operated on-site, and a dedicated shuttle bus system transported workers across the sprawling facility.

155e4ed48f.q: How does union administration and regulatory oversight affect industry culture and worker protection?
155e4ed48f.a: Ray states: I honestly don't think so about the current administration changing industry culture. He argues that the overreach of government with Mr Irving's administration is a national disgrace, similar to the parameters of the ABCC, where murderers and rapists had more rights than construction workers. He believes the union must protect members when money is floating around, but that government only wants monuments to justify their time in power and doesn't take responsibility for what happens on their watch.
f: No, changing administrations won't shift industry culture on its own. Government overreach causes far more harm to workers than administrative shifts —Ray Smith compares the current era to the ABCC period, where construction workers had fewer rights than convicted murderers and rapists.

Ray Smith's perspective challenges the notion that simply rotating leadership or adjusting regulatory frameworks will meaningfully protect workers or reshape how the industry operates. The real damage, he argues, comes from government bodies that prioritize monuments to their own legacy over accountability for the conditions workers face on site.

Government agencies, Smith contends, pursue agendas that benefit the state rather than the workforce. They seek visible projects to justify their tenure but accept no responsibility for workplace deaths, injuries, or exploitation that occurs during execution. This structural indifference places the burden of member protection entirely on unions themselves.

Ray Smith — Construction Worker, Delegate, and Tour Manager. After spending nearly 30 years in the music industry from the mid-1970s to the mid-1990s—working as a roadie and tour manager for acts including Cold Chisel, the Rolling Stones, Joe Cocker, and Oasis—Smith transitioned to construction. He became a delegate representing union members across mixed metals, civil engineering, building, and infrastructure projects in Melbourne and regional Victoria, gaining decades of direct experience navigating union-management relations and regulatory frameworks.

In the episode, Smith explores the specific parallels between the ABCC era and modern regulatory overreach , drawing on his lived experience as both a worker and a union representative. His argument rests on a simple premise: **unions must be the primary safeguard for members** because governments will never take genuine responsibility for worker safety or dignity.

The implication is stark. Industry culture shifts only when union power remains strong and vigilant—not when governments change personnel or issue new policies. Protecting workers requires constant defense against both negligent employers and government bodies that view construction sites as mere backdrops for political achievement rather than spaces where human lives are at stake.

890e4900a4.q: What is the trajectory of the union's role and influence in Australia's construction sector long-term?
890e4900a4.a: Ray believes the industry is still in a very strong position and that anyone thinking they will deregister the organisation and pull the timbers from under it should dream on, because for as long as there are people doing what they do, there's most certainly a role for the unions to play. He expresses frustration that unions deal with problems, fatalities, injuries, and rip-offs while being blamed.
f: The construction union will remain indispensable as long as workers exist —Ray Smith firmly rejects any notion that deregulation could undermine its necessity. Unions deal with fatalities, injuries, and worker exploitation while facing undeserved criticism; the solution is not to dismantle them, but to recognize their vital protective function.

Ray Smith's conviction rests on a straightforward principle: workers will always require collective representation . In his view, the union's future is secure not because of regulatory mandates, but because the fundamental challenges it addresses—safety violations, wage theft, workplace injuries—remain endemic to the industry. As long as these problems persist, the organization that fights them will remain necessary.

The frustration Smith expresses is revealing. Unions handle the difficult work of confronting fatalities, injuries, and systematic rip-offs while being blamed for perceived rigidity or obstruction. This inversion of responsibility—where the problem-solver faces criticism instead of the problem itself—points to a deeper misunderstanding of the union's role in the sector, as discussed in detail in this episode of Creatures of the Industry .
"For as long as there are people doing what they do, there's most certainly a role for the unions to play."

Ray Smith — Construction Worker, Delegate, and Tour Manager. Smith spent nearly 30 years in the music industry starting around 1975–1976, working as a roadie, manager, and tour manager for major acts including Johnny Diesel and the Injectors, Cold Chisel, the Rolling Stones, Joe Cocker, and Oasis. He later transitioned into the construction sector, where he became a delegate representing union members across Melbourne and regional Victoria, gaining hands-on experience in mixed metals, civil engineering, building, and infrastructure projects. His dual career background gives him unique perspective on organizational culture and worker solidarity across industries.

Smith's position directly challenges deregulation arguments that suggest removing union oversight would liberate the industry. His counterpoint is pragmatic: deregulation addresses none of the actual harms unions exist to prevent. Fatalities do not disappear when enforcement structures weaken; if anything, they multiply. The trajectory he envisions is one in which unions evolve in response to changing industry conditions, but never become obsolete because the need for worker protection does not become obsolete.

1a9d37452b.q: What career path led Ray 'Rowdy' Smith from music industry management to construction work?
1a9d37452b.a: Ray spent nearly 30 years in the music industry, leaving school around 1975-1976, working as a roadie carrying black boxes and eventually becoming a manager. His father played drums and was interested in music and bands. Ray was determined to play in a band and be part of the industry, and went on to manage Johnny Diesel and the Injectors, who achieved major success, becoming the first band in Australia to sell half a million copies. He transitioned to construction after leaving the music touring circuit.
f: Ray Smith left school around 1975–1976 and spent nearly 30 years in the music industry as a roadie and manager , working with acts including Johnny Diesel and the Injectors—the first Australian band to sell half a million copies. He eventually stepped away from the touring circuit and moved into construction, where he discovered a deeper sense of belonging through the camaraderie and union representation work that followed.
From Roadie to Tour Manager

Ray's entry into the music world was deeply personal. His father played drums and was active in bands, inspiring young Ray to pursue a career in the industry rather than a conventional path. He began as a roadie carrying equipment at venues, earning modest wages—around five to ten dollars per night during the 1970s and 80s—while working five to seven nights a week. Over time, he developed the skills and relationships that elevated him to tour management.

His management portfolio became impressive: Ray worked with Johnny Diesel and the Injectors during their rise to national prominence, and also handled touring logistics for major international acts including Cold Chisel, the Rolling Stones, Joe Cocker, and Oasis. The details of managing these high-profile tours are explored further in the episode , offering insights into the demands of the touring lifestyle in that era.
The Move to Construction

Ray's transition to construction was not a sudden break but a deliberate step away from the touring circuit. When he first entered the industry, he thought it would be a temporary 12-month engagement —a way to try something new before returning to music management. That plan changed.

8a98a9d4c8.q: What was the scale of success achieved by Johnny Diesel and the Injectors in the Australian music market?
8a98a9d4c8.a: Johnny Diesel and the Injectors were the first band in Australia to sell half a million copies, holding that title for a few years until John Farnham's The Voice superseded them with higher sales. The band secured a record deal from America in 1998, and Ray along with the band lived in Memphis, Tennessee for about 8 months where they recorded their first album.

62bbb8bacc.q: How did Ray Smith manage high-profile touring artists and what challenges did he encounter?
62bbb8bacc.a: Ray toured with major international acts including the Rolling Stones and Joe Cocker, becoming good friends with Cocker who would ring him whenever he toured Australia. Ray was Oasis's Australian tour manager during their early tour, and had to manage a Gallagher brother who was disruptive at Sydney Entertainment Centre. Ray ultimately decided to leave touring because of the constant airports, tour buses, planes, trains, and everything in between, which took him a long time to recover from.
f: Ray Smith toured with major international acts including the Rolling Stones and Joe Cocker, becoming close friends with Cocker who would call him whenever he toured Australia. During Oasis's early Australian tour, Smith managed a disruptive Gallagher brother at Sydney Entertainment Centre , but ultimately left touring after nearly 30 years because the constant airports, tour buses, planes, and trains made recovery nearly impossible.
From roadie to tour manager: nearly three decades on the road

Ray Smith began his music industry career around 1975-1976 as a roadie, carrying equipment and building experience with bands like Johnny Diesel and the Injectors, Cold Chisel, and Georgia Satellites. Over nearly 30 years in the touring circuit , he progressed from roadie to manager and eventually tour manager, handling logistics and artist relations for some of the biggest names in international rock and pop. This long tenure gave him deep insight into the realities of high-profile touring.

His work with major acts like the Rolling Stones and Joe Cocker demonstrated his ability to manage complex touring operations at the highest level. As Smith explains in the podcast , the personal relationships that formed during this time—particularly his friendship with Joe Cocker—were as significant as the professional achievements. Cocker trusted Smith enough to ring him directly whenever his tours came to Australia.
Managing the Gallagher brothers and the cost of constant travel

When Oasis came to Australia for their early tour, Smith took on the role of Australian tour manager. One Gallagher brother proved particularly disruptive at Sydney Entertainment Centre , requiring Smith to navigate the tensions and unpredictability that can arise when managing high-ego artists on the road. These moments tested his management skills under real pressure.

d4c279c2e9.q: What approach did Ray Smith take when confronted with disrespectful behavior from a touring artist?
d4c279c2e9.a: When a Gallagher brother from Oasis was carrying on rudely at Sydney Entertainment Centre about the third night of their tour, Ray politely bumped him into a room and said: if we're going to work together, you're going to learn to be a bit more respectful in the way you talk to people. I don't know how you talk to your old man, but you won't be talking to me like that. The artist's London management later praised Ray for being the first to pull the artist in line, and the next day the artist apologized.
f: Ray Smith pulled a Gallagher brother from Oasis into a private room during their Sydney Entertainment Centre tour and calmly laid out expectations: respect is non-negotiable when working together . He made it clear that disrespectful behavior wouldn't be tolerated, and the next day, the artist apologized. The artist's London management later thanked Smith for being the first person to establish that boundary.

What made Smith's approach effective wasn't aggression—it was directness combined with professionalism. He didn't shame the artist publicly or escalate the situation. Instead, he removed him from the immediate environment and communicated a simple truth: mutual respect is the foundation of any working relationship.

This moment reveals a principle that Smith had clearly learned during nearly 30 years managing touring musicians —confrontation works best when it's grounded in respect for the other person, even when you're correcting them. Smith treated the artist as someone capable of change, not someone to be written off.

The apology the next day wasn't forced or defensive. It came from genuine recognition that the artist had crossed a line. In touring, where weeks on the road can amplify tension and ego, having a tour manager willing to reset standards is rare. Smith's willingness to have that difficult conversation, rather than letting bad behavior slide, ultimately strengthened the working relationship.

f: The Coot Island redevelopment site contained PFAS chemical residue from a historical fire that had leached into the subsoil , contamination that persists to this day. The groundworks uncovered buried materials alongside this chemical contamination, and the severity of the issue was significant enough to later impact the nearby Westgate project.

When Ray Smith arrived at Coot Island in January 2004 for his first construction job—transitioning from the music industry—the site was already in redevelopment. The environmental challenges hidden beneath the surface only became apparent once excavation work began.
PFAS persistence and cross-project impact

The contamination discovered at Coot Island was not isolated to that single site. The PFAS chemicals that seeped into the subsoil created a broader environmental concern that extended beyond the immediate redevelopment boundaries. As work progressed on subsequent projects in the area, this legacy contamination resurfaced as a complicating factor.

This is a point detailed in the episode , where Ray Smith reflects on the tangible obstacles that environmental remediation posed to construction crews. The discovery of chemical residue mixed with buried materials required workers to navigate both physical and regulatory challenges on site.
